description.summary: A former tuberculosis sanatorium in Louisville, Kentucky (opened 1910, expanded 1926, closed 1961) widely reputed to be haunted; among the most heavily investigated 'haunted hospital' locations in the United States.
description.full: Waverly Hills Sanatorium is a former tuberculosis hospital in the Waverly Hills neighborhood of Louisville, Kentucky. The original two-story wooden facility opened in 1910 and was replaced by a much larger five-story Gothic Revival brick building that opened on October 17, 1926. Following the introduction of the antibiotic streptomycin in 1943 and improvements in TB treatment, the sanatorium closed in June 1961; the building reopened the next year as the Woodhaven Geriatric Center, which the Commonwealth of Kentucky shut down in 1980/1982. Since being purchased by Tina and Charlie Mattingly in 2001, the site has been preserved as a paranormal-tourism attraction and a Halloween haunted-attraction venue, with proceeds going toward restoration. Waverly Hills was added to the U.S. National Register of Historic Places on July 12, 1983. Its reputation as a haunted location is sustained by reports of full-bodied apparitions, shadow figures, disembodied voices, and physical contact, and by appearances on television programmes including Ghost Hunters and Ghost Adventures and in the 2005 horror film Death Tunnel. The building includes a service tunnel — the so-called 'body chute' or 'death tunnel' — that connected the heating plant to the main building and is the focus of much of the site's modern legend, although mainstream historical accounts describe it as a service and supply tunnel that may also have been used to discreetly remove the bodies of deceased patients.

etymology.origin: Named for the Waverly Hills neighborhood of Louisville; the area was reportedly named for Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels by an early-19th-century schoolteacher, Major Thomas H. Hays.
etymology.meaning: Place-name derived from the early-19th-century literary Waverley association.
etymology.first_use: The sanatorium opened under the name Waverly Hills in 1910.

related_phenomena.name: Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum
related_phenomena.description: Comparable U.S. former-institutional haunted-tourism site (West Virginia)

features.feature: Five-story Gothic Revival brick main building
features.description: Opened October 17, 1926 to replace the 1910 wooden facility; capable of housing more than 400 TB patients
A service tunnel running roughly 500 ft from the main building to the bottom of the hill, originally built to carry steam, supplies, and (according to local tradition) the bodies of deceased patients
Wide screened porches characteristic of pre-antibiotic TB sanatoriums, intended to expose patients to fresh air and sunlight

physical.morphology: A large early-20th-century institutional hospital complex on a wooded hilltop, partially restored and partially in arrested decay.

habitat_preference: patient wards on the fourth and fifth floors
patterns: Reports cluster on the fourth and fifth floors and in the body-chute tunnel
Reports include named figures such as 'Timmy' (a child apparition) and a 'creeper' or 'shadow figure'
Activity is reported by both staff/owners and visiting investigators

range.description: A single fixed location: the Waverly Hills Sanatorium complex on Paralee Drive, Louisville, Kentucky.

hotspots.name: Waverly Hills Sanatorium main building
hotspots.notes: The main 1926 Gothic Revival building is the focus of nearly all reported phenomena and investigations.

first_recorded.source: Original wooden Waverly Hills tuberculosis hospital opened 1910

peak_activity_periods.description: TB sanatorium era; large patient population and high in-house mortality before antibiotic therapy
Modern paranormal-tourism and investigation era under Mattingly ownership

origins.cultural_roots: Early-20th-century American public health response to the tuberculosis epidemic, particularly the open-air sanatorium movement.
origins.earliest_accounts: The original wooden Waverly Hills tuberculosis hospital opened in 1910; the much larger Gothic Revival facility opened on October 17, 1926.
origins.folklore_connections: Modern legend of Waverly Hills draws on a wider American tradition of haunted hospitals and asylums (e.g., Trans-Allegheny Lunatic Asylum, Danvers State Hospital).

timeline.event: Original wooden Waverly Hills tuberculosis hospital opens in Louisville, Kentucky
New five-story Gothic Revival brick sanatorium opens
Streptomycin antibiotic introduced for tuberculosis treatment, eventually allowing TB patients to be treated as outpatients
timeline.significance: Begins the obsolescence of large TB sanatoriums

timeline.event: Waverly Hills closes as a tuberculosis sanatorium
Building reopens as the Woodhaven Geriatric Center
Commonwealth of Kentucky closes the Woodhaven Geriatric Center after allegations of mistreatment of patients
timeline.significance: End of the building's institutional use

timeline.event: Waverly Hills Sanatorium added to the U.S. National Register of Historic Places
Tina and Charlie Mattingly purchase the property
timeline.significance: Begin the long-running restoration / paranormal-tourism era

history.modern_era: Under the Mattinglys' stewardship, Waverly Hills hosts paranormal investigations, public ghost tours, and a major Halloween haunted-attraction season; television appearances on Ghost Hunters (2006), Ghost Adventures, BuzzFeed Unsolved, and others have made it one of the most-visited haunted-hospital sites in the United States.

documentary.name: U.S. National Register of Historic Places listing (1983)
documentary.description: Federal heritage listing recognising the historical importance of the Waverly Hills Sanatorium complex.
documentary.analysis: Independently confirms the building's history and significance as a TB sanatorium.
documentary.source: U.S. National Register of Historic Places

documentary.name: Ghost Hunters (TAPS) Waverly Hills episode
documentary.description: Investigation of Waverly Hills by The Atlantic Paranormal Society for the SyFy series Ghost Hunters.
documentary.analysis: Most-cited televised paranormal investigation of the site; widely treated as entertainment rather than scientific evidence.

paranormal.name: Residual hauntings from TB-era deaths
paranormal.description: Reported phenomena are interpreted as the residue of large numbers of patient deaths during the TB era, particularly on the fourth and fifth floors.
evidence_cited: Reports of apparitions, shadow figures, disembodied voices, and physical contact across multiple decades and groups

skeptical.name: Suggestion, expectation, and pareidolia in a high-suggestion environment
skeptical.description: Skeptics hold that the building's known reputation, dim lighting, ambient infrasound, and visitors' expectations sufficiently account for reported experiences without invoking the paranormal.
evidence_cited: Pattern of reports clustering with public-tour and television activity
Lack of independently reproducible paranormal data

skeptical.name: Inflated 'death-toll' figures
skeptical.description: The widely repeated claim that over 60,000 people died at Waverly Hills is rejected by historians and the property's owners as far higher than the actual death toll.

stories: The 'body chute' / 'death tunnel' as a route for discreetly removing TB victims' bodies
Apparition stories of 'Timmy', a child ghost said to play with a ball on the third floor
Reports of a tall 'creeper' shadow figure
folklore.beliefs: Local and online communities widely treat Waverly Hills as one of the most active haunted locations in the United States; mainstream history and skeptical scholarship treat the haunting reputation as cultural rather than evidential.

literature: Charlie & Janie Mattingly, with the Waverly Hills Historical Society — public history materials

research.ongoing_studies: Active paranormal-investigation programmes (visiting groups), restoration work, and historical research; no peer-reviewed paranormal research is conducted at the site.
